title: Breaking News Homepage
prompt: A news site's homepage is read far more often than its database can serve. Editors want breaking news to appear on the homepage quickly. Design the read path for the homepage.
facts: Peak: about 20,000 homepage reads per second
The database serves about 2,000 reads per second and should run at no more than two thirds of that at peak
A new story must appear on the homepage within 30 seconds of publishing
Building the homepage from the database takes at most 2 seconds, including storing it in the cache
The homepage is the same for every reader
scope: Article pages and personalization are out of scope
The 30-second freshness applies while the database works; a database outage is out of scope

requirements: States the 30-second freshness requirement and the database limit
Notes that every reader sees the same page, so one cache entry serves everyone
estimation: Database budget: 2,000 × 2 ÷ 3 ≈ 1,333 reads per second; with cache-aside, misses may be at most 1,333 ÷ 20,000 ≈ 6.7%, so a hit rate of at least about 93.4%
Or, with a refresh job, database load is one build per refresh interval

Freshness budget for the chosen policy: if readers wait for a rebuild after expiry, a copy can be 2 s old when stored, so TTL ≤ 28 s; if the old copy is served while one server rebuilds, add the rebuild: 2 + TTL + 2 ≤ 30, so TTL ≤ 26 s; for a job every N seconds, N + 2 ≤ 30
design: Servers read the homepage from a cache before the database, filled by cache-aside or by a refresh job
data: One cache key for the homepage with a TTL inside the freshness budget, or a job that rebuilds it on a fixed interval
Explains why the hit rate stays high or why database load stays low
tradeoffs: Names a risk with its condition, such as: when the key expires, many servers miss at once and hit the database (thundering herd), so only one server rebuilds; or if the refresh job stops, the page goes stale, so servers rebuild it themselves early enough to stay within 30 s; or a shorter TTL gives fresher news but more rebuilds

fullMarkDesigns: Design A, cache-aside: servers read the homepage key; on a miss only one server rebuilds it while the others serve the old copy, and the new copy gets a TTL of 20 s. Freshness: 2 + 20 + 2 = 24 s, within 30. Database load: one rebuild per expiry, far under 1,333 reads per second, so the hit rate is close to 100% (≥ 93.4% needed). Risk: thundering herd at expiry, prevented by the single rebuilder.

Design B, refresh job: a job rebuilds the homepage every 10 s and writes it to the cache; servers only read the cache. Freshness: 10 + 2 = 12 s. Database load: one build every 10 s. Trade-off: the job is a new part; servers check the copy's age on every read, and if it is older than 25 s (the job has stopped) one server rebuilds it, so news is at most 2 + 25 + 2 = 29 s old, and an alert is raised.

assumptions: Every reader gets the same homepage
The cache is in the same data center as the servers
reference.design:
Servers read the homepage from the cache. On a miss, a single server rebuilds it from the database (at most 2 s) and stores it with a TTL of 20 s; other servers keep serving the previous copy until the new one is ready.
Database budget: 2,000 × 2 ÷ 3 ≈ 1,333 reads per second, so at most about 6.7% of 20,000 reads may miss (a hit rate of at least about 93.4%). With one key, misses happen only at expiry, so the hit rate is close to 100%.
Freshness: a copy can be 2 s old when stored, is served for 20 s, and may be served 2 s more while the next one is built: 24 s, inside 30 s.
alternatives: A refresh job every 10 seconds: freshness about 12 s and no misses, but one more part to watch
Invalidating the key when an editor publishes: fresher, but every publish must reach the cache reliably

title: Travel Blog Photos Worldwide
prompt: A travel blog stores its photos on one origin server in Singapore. Readers in Europe and the United States complain that photos load slowly. Design how photos are delivered.
facts: About 2 million photo requests per day from Asia, Europe and the United States; peak is about 5 times the average
Photos average about 200 KB; the origin server can send about 300 photos per second
A round trip from Europe or the United States to Singapore takes about 160–220 ms; loading a photo from Singapore on a new connection takes about 3 round trips plus the transfer
A CDN has edge servers in Europe and the United States; from a nearby edge, a cached 200 KB photo loads in about 100 ms
Photos never change after upload; an edited photo is uploaded under a new file name
Requirement: a photo served from an edge's cached copy loads within 300 ms. A first request in a region, or a request after the edge's copy expired, goes to Singapore and may be slower
Exercise assumption: an edge keeps a photo until its TTL ends, counted from when the edge fetched it from the origin; most views of a photo happen in the month after it is posted
scope: The blog's text pages are out of scope

requirements: States the 300 ms requirement for photos served from an edge's copy, and that first requests and requests after expiry may be slower
estimation: Distance: 3 round trips × 160 ms = 480 ms or more before the transfer, over 300 ms, so meeting it needs a nearby copy; a cached copy at an edge takes about 100 ms
Or load: 2 × 10⁶ ÷ 10⁵ = 20 photos per second on average, about 100 at peak, under the origin's 300, so the problem is distance, not origin load
design: Readers → CDN edge server in their region → origin in Singapore on a miss
data: A TTL that keeps photos at the edge through the month most views happen, made safe by never changing a photo under the same name
Explains that the first request in a region is a miss and goes to the origin
tradeoffs: Names a trade-off with its condition, such as: the first request for a photo in each region is slow, which the requirement allows; or a deleted photo stays on edges until it expires or is purged; or a shorter TTL with revalidation makes removals quick but sends more requests to Singapore

fullMarkDesigns: Design A: a CDN in front of the origin with a one-year TTL; edited photos get new file names, so no invalidation is needed. Repeat requests in a region load from the edge in about 100 ms. Distance estimate: 3 × 160 = 480 ms from Singapore, too slow without the edge. Trade-off: removing a photo needs a CDN purge.

Design B: a CDN with a 7-day TTL; when the edge's copy expires, the next request in that region checks with the origin and is slow, then the copy is cached for another week. A removed photo disappears within a week even without a purge. Load estimate: about 100 photos per second at peak, under the origin's 300, so the weekly re-checks are affordable. Trade-off: each popular photo has one slow request per region per week, which the requirement allows.

assumptions: Most photos are read many times in each region
An edge keeps a photo until its TTL ends
reference.design:
Readers fetch photos from a CDN. The nearest edge server returns a cached copy in about 100 ms; on a miss it fetches the photo from the origin in Singapore and keeps it.
Because photos never change and an edit gets a new file name, the TTL can be very long, so edges almost never go back to the origin.
Distance is the problem: 3 round trips × 160–220 ms is 480 ms or more from Singapore. Load is not: about 20 photos per second on average and 100 at peak, under the origin's 300.
The first request for a photo in a region still crosses to Singapore, which the requirement allows.
alternatives: A 7-day TTL with revalidation: removed photos disappear within a week, at the cost of some requests to Singapore
A second origin server in Europe: fixes Europe only and must be kept in sync
